blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Text-to-image diffusion models can produce unsafe content, while output filtering intervenes only after synthesis. We investigate whether native generation signals enable early detection of unsafe and adversarial inputs. We find that classifier-free guidance exposes strong safety signals in conditional responses, accessible through compact statistics and linear readouts. Based on this finding, we propose Conditional Semantic Trajectory Interception (CSTI), which aggregates activation contrasts between conditional and unconditional responses at early checkpoints for calibrated risk detection. CSTI fits concept-specific detectors using canonical concept and safe examples, without attack samples, intermediate image decoding, or generator modification. Across five generators, four adversarial attack collections, and two general NSFW datasets, CSTI achieves the strongest overall performance among six baselines at a matched 5% FPR. Early interception reduces generation latency by over 60% on intercepted paths. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of native conditional responses for early safety interception.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Safety mechanisms for text-to-image generation operate at different
stages. Before sampling, text classifiers such as the NSFW Text
Classifier [ 21 ] and
Detoxify [ 11 ] can screen potentially unsafe requests.
Latent Guard [ 18 ] detects harmful concepts
in learned representations of text encoder embeddings, while
GuardT2I [ 44 ] uses a language model to convert
text guidance embeddings into natural language for adversarial
prompt detection.
Such screening can reject risky requests before synthesis, but does
not observe how the generative state develops during sampling.
Other defenses change how images are generated.
ESD [ 7 ] removes target concepts by updating
model weights, whereas SLD [ 24 ] and
CRG [ 5 ] suppress unsafe concepts through
inference-time guidance.
Adversarial methods such as Ring-A-Bell [ 31 ] and MMA-Diffusion [ 43 ] demonstrate that
crafted prompts can still elicit unsafe outputs despite existing
safeguards.
Together, these approaches motivate examining whether risk can be
assessed during generation without changing accepted sampling.
Table 1 compares representative
defenses according to their observation and intervention mechanisms.

blocks.en:
Recent methods inspect intermediate model states to identify unsafe
content before the final image is available.
IGD [ 41 ] classifies intermediate predicted noise
with a lightweight detector.
Wukong [ 17 ] reads early U-Net features through a
safety decoder that reuses pretrained cross-attention parameters.
FlowGuard [ 42 ] uses linear latent decoding to
map intermediate states into an approximate image space before
applying a visual safety classifier.
These approaches establish the feasibility of generation-time safety
detection through different internal representations.
Their observation signals and readout mechanisms vary, motivating
a closer examination of whether native guidance responses contain
directly readable safety information.
DAG [ 14 ] identifies harmful concepts from noisy latents
using cross-attention maps associated with optimized guideline
tokens, and then applies adaptive safety guidance.
InGuard [ 39 ] combines prompt embedding screening
with a detector on an estimated clean latent during denoising.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We investigated early safety signals in text-to-image
diffusion models and found that native conditional
responses enable effective detection of unsafe and
adversarial inputs through compact statistics and
simple linear readouts. Building on this finding,
we introduced CSTI for calibrated early interception
without attack samples, intermediate image decoding,
or modification of accepted sampling.
Experiments across five generators spanning U-Net
and Transformer architectures demonstrate strong
overall detection performance against representative
baselines. Further analyses show that safety signals
are accessible at early sampling stages and across
multiple layers, while simple linear readouts remain
effective. These findings demonstrate that native
guidance computation provides an effective and
efficient foundation for early safety interception.

blocks.en:
The security of deep learning systems has been extensively
investigated across diverse adversarial settings.
Existing research has explored adversarial perturbations
and robustness [ 8 , 20 , 2 , 13 ] , as well as transferable attacks
against visual and multimodal representations [ 27 , 26 , 37 ] .
Related studies have also investigated adversarial
manipulation of training data and learned representations,
including unlearnable examples [ 33 , 36 ] .
Beyond inference-time attacks, training-time threats such
as data poisoning and model poisoning [ 52 , 15 ] , as well as
backdoor attacks [ 10 , 56 , 50 ] , can compromise learned representations
and induce unintended model behaviors.
Corresponding detection mechanisms have also been
investigated across different learning architectures
and tasks [ 45 , 51 ] .
These efforts highlight the broader importance of
identifying adversarially induced behavior and developing
reliable safeguards for increasingly capable AI systems.

As AI systems integrate language, vision, and decision-making
capabilities, safety concerns have expanded beyond
conventional discriminative prediction.
Recent research has examined jailbreak attacks against
large language models [ 57 , 53 ] , adversarial prompting and prompt

Related security challenges also arise in visual generative

misleading content [ 40 , 46 ] .
While these settings differ in their threat models and
attack objectives, they underscore the need for safety
mechanisms that extend beyond conventional input screening.
In particular, generative models progressively construct
their outputs through multiple computational stages,
raising the question of whether emerging risks can be
identified before synthesis is complete.

blocks.en:
Safety mechanisms for text-to-image generation operate at
different stages of the generation pipeline.
Before sampling, text classifiers such as the NSFW Text
Classifier [ 21 ] and
Detoxify [ 11 ] can screen potentially unsafe
requests.
Latent Guard [ 18 ] detects harmful
concepts in text encoder representations, while
GuardT2I [ 44 ] examines textual
interpretations of guidance embeddings for adversarial
prompt detection.
Such screening can reject risky requests before synthesis,
but does not observe how the generative state evolves
during sampling.
Other defenses directly modify the generation process.
ESD [ 7 ] removes target concepts
by updating model weights, whereas
SLD [ 24 ] and
CRG [ 5 ] suppress unsafe concepts through
inference-time guidance.
Nevertheless, adversarial prompting approaches such as
Ring-A-Bell [ 31 ] and
MMA-Diffusion [ 43 ] demonstrate
that unsafe content can still be elicited despite
existing safeguards.
These limitations motivate safety assessment during
generation, without modifying accepted sampling
trajectories.

Recent studies investigate whether intermediate diffusion
states can reveal safety-relevant information before the
final image is available.
IGD [ 41 ] classifies intermediate predicted
noise, while Wukong [ 17 ] detects unsafe

for harmful concept identification and adaptive guidance,
whereas InGuard [ 39 ] combines prompt
screening with detection on estimated clean latents.
These approaches demonstrate the feasibility of assessing
generation risk from intermediate computations, although
their observation signals and intervention mechanisms
differ.

blocks.en:
In contrast to approaches that require intermediate
image reconstruction, auxiliary safety decoders, or
modification of the generation process, CSTI examines
the paired conditional and unconditional activations
already computed by classifier-free guidance.
By aggregating compact channel statistics across early
sampling checkpoints, CSTI extracts safety-relevant
signals using a lightweight linear readout.
An independent safe calibration set determines the
interception threshold, while flagged generations
terminate early and accepted trajectories remain
unchanged.
This design exploits native conditional computation
to support efficient safety assessment before
image synthesis is complete.
